tagline: From reservoir country to mill buildings and a turnpike settlement.
intro: Falls Road carries the drive from rural country near Alesia into Baltimore, following MD 25 through the Jones Falls Valley. It belongs to Maryland’s scenic-byway system, with Prettyboy Reservoir near its northern end and city neighborhoods at the other. A westward spur on MD 130 reaches the Green Spring Valley area, where the historic district includes buildings from the eighteenth century through the early twentieth.

Along the older Falls Turnpike, industry and settlement grew together. At Bare Hills, the National Register registration document records that Aquila Scott bought two acres in 1839 and established a blacksmith shop and home fronting the turnpike. His children built homes on the tract as they formed families, creating Scott’s Settlement. The Maryland Historical Trust traces Bare Hills from milling and mining through its turnpike era to residential development, after rail service made commuting into Baltimore possible.

Driving south from Alesia, pass the Prettyboy Reservoir area, Butler and Oregon Ridge Park before reaching the more developed stretch toward Baltimore. Rockland’s mill district occupies the junction with Old Court Road and Ruxton Road. Continue past Bare Hills toward Mount Washington and Roland Park, then the neighborhoods of Woodberry, Brick Hill and Hampden.

moments.title: Prettyboy Reservoir
moments.text: Water stored at Prettyboy takes an indirect route to Baltimore’s taps. The dam, completed in 1932, holds back the Gunpowder Falls; water then travels downstream to Loch Raven Reservoir. From there, a tunnel carries it to the Montebello Filtration Plants for treatment and distribution. Although Prettyboy lies in Baltimore County, the city owns both the reservoir and its surrounding land. The reservoir is part of a three-reservoir system created to supply Baltimore City, Baltimore County and northern Anne Arundel County. Prettyboy covers 1,500 acres in the Hereford Zone of northern Baltimore County.

moments.title: Rockland
moments.text: The grist mill at Rockland had a working life that reached far beyond grain. Dating to at least 1810, it has housed calico manufacture, cotton spinning, and the production of wooden toys and artificial silk. The surrounding district preserves an early nineteenth-century community at the meeting of Falls, Old Court and Ruxton roads. Its fifteen buildings include stone rowhouses, log buildings, a carriage house and the shell of a blacksmith shop. The district entered the National Register in 1973 and underwent restoration in 1982. The mill’s later products also included food-preservation additives and jewelry-cleaning solutions.
moments.notice: Stone rowhouses and log buildings share the district with the grist mill.

moments.title: Bare Hills
moments.text: A blacksmith’s two-acre property became the nucleus of Scott’s Settlement. The National Register registration document identifies Aquila Scott as a blacksmith and Methodist preacher who arrived by 1830, then bought land beside the Falls Turnpike in 1839. His children built houses there as their own families grew. The Maryland Historical Trust identifies the settlement as one of Baltimore County’s earliest free Black communities. It ties the Bare Hills name to a serpentine-rock formation that the Jones Falls bends around on its way toward Baltimore. Scott’s original log church burned in 1876; its surviving replacement was built in 1886, across Lake Roland and outside the historic district.
